name: LLM Caching and Routing
intent: Cut the cost and latency of LLM calls by reusing work (response and prefix caches) and by sending each request to the cheapest model that can answer it.
scenario: A SaaS support assistant sends every question with an 800-token prompt (600 tokens of shared system prompt and policy text, 200 of question) and gets about 150 tokens back. On a large model that is about $0.0047 and 2 seconds per question. Many questions repeat or paraphrase, and most are easy, but a naive cache sometimes returns the answer to a different question.
problem: LLM calls are slow and billed per token. Output tokens are generated one at a time, so latency grows with answer length, and long prompts cost money on every call even when 75% of them is identical text. Large models are 10 to 50 times more expensive per token than small ones, yet most traffic does not need them. Caching and routing can remove most of the bill, but a cache that matches by meaning can return confidently wrong answers, and a router that trusts a model's confidence can ship wrong answers cheaply.

howItWorks.title: Know where the cost comes from
howItWorks.text: Price is roughly input tokens times input rate plus output tokens times output rate, and output tokens usually cost 3 to 6 times more each. Latency is a prefill pass (reading the whole prompt) plus one sequential decode step (writing one token) per output token. At 800 input and 150 output tokens, a large model costs on the order of a cent or less per call and 1 to 3 seconds; a small model is often 10 to 30 times cheaper and 3 to 5 times faster. Rates and speeds vary by provider and change often, so keep them in config, not code.

howItWorks.title: Exact-match response cache
howItWorks.text: Hash the normalized request (model, system prompt, parameters, user text, and the tenant, meaning the customer account) and store the response, as in any cache. A hit costs a lookup and is always correct for deterministic use. It only helps when identical requests repeat (FAQ buttons, retries, batch re-runs), and it is useless for free text, which rarely repeats byte for byte. Only cache when the answer does not depend on hidden state, and set a TTL (time to live, how long an entry may be reused) tied to how fast the underlying facts change.

howItWorks.title: Prompt-prefix (KV) caching
howItWorks.text: Providers and self-hosted servers can reuse the attention state (the KV cache) computed for a prompt prefix, so a repeated 600-token system prompt is not recomputed and is typically billed at a discount. It only matches an identical prefix, token for token, from the start. Put stable content first (system prompt, tools, documents) and volatile content last (timestamp, user id, the question). One changed token early in the prompt invalidates everything after it. Entries expire after minutes of inactivity, so it pays off for steady traffic, not for rare calls.

howItWorks.title: Semantic cache by embedding similarity
howItWorks.text: Embed the question (turn it into a list of numbers that captures its meaning), find the nearest stored question, and return its answer if cosine similarity (a score of how alike two embeddings are) is above a threshold. This catches paraphrases that exact matching misses, but similarity measures topical closeness, not equivalence: "refund within 30 days" and "refund within 3 days" can score above 0.95. Choose the threshold from labelled pairs of your own traffic, scope entries per tenant and per prompt version, give them TTLs, and measure the wrong-hit rate, and not only the hit rate.

howItWorks.title: Route by difficulty: a cascade
howItWorks.text: Send the request to a cheap model first and accept its answer when a signal says it is good enough (a self-reported or calibrated confidence, a verifier, a classifier on the question, or answer-format checks); otherwise escalate to the large model. Cost is the cheap call for everyone plus the large call for the escalated share. It works when most traffic is easy and the signal is reliable; it fails quietly when the cheap model is confidently wrong. A classifier that routes before calling any model avoids paying twice but needs its own training and evaluation.

howItWorks.title: Fallbacks, budgets and limits
howItWorks.text: Providers rate-limit by requests and by tokens per minute and return 429 (too many requests) or 5xx under load. Retry with backoff and jitter (growing, slightly random waits), fail over to another provider or a smaller model, and degrade honestly (shorter answer, cached answer with a note) rather than erroring. Enforce per-request token caps (max input, max output), per-tenant daily budgets, and a global spend alarm, because a loop or a long-context abuse can burn a month of budget in an hour.

pros: Caching removes whole calls: a hit takes a few milliseconds and costs nearly nothing
Prefix caching cuts the cost and time-to-first-token of long shared prompts with no change in answers
Cascades can cut cost by half or more when most traffic is easy
Fallbacks keep the feature up through provider rate limits and outages
cons: Semantic caches and cheap-model routing trade money for wrong answers, and the wrong answers are fluent and look right
Hit rate depends on traffic: unique, long-tail questions barely cache
More moving parts: embedding model, vector index, thresholds, TTLs, confidence calibration, per-tenant scoping
Quality now depends on evaluation you must keep running, because model versions, prompts and traffic drift
whenToUse: High volume with repeated or paraphrased questions (support, search suggestions, FAQ bots)
Long shared prompts: system instructions, tool definitions or a document asked about many times
Mixed difficulty traffic where a small model handles most requests
Any production LLM feature that needs a spend ceiling and a plan for provider outages
whenNotToUse: Low volume, where the engineering and evaluation effort costs more than the savings
Personalised, time-sensitive or high-stakes answers (account balances, medical, legal, money movement) where a stale or near-miss answer is unacceptable
Highly diverse inputs where nothing repeats; start with prefix caching and a smaller model instead
When you cannot measure answer quality; you would be saving money blind
pitfalls: Putting a timestamp, request id or user name at the top of the prompt, which invalidates the prefix cache on every call
Choosing the similarity threshold by looking at hit rate alone; measure wrong-hit rate on labelled near-miss pairs, and note that good thresholds depend on the embedding model
A shared semantic cache across tenants or users, which can serve one customer's data to another
No TTL or no invalidation when the source documents or the system prompt change, so stale answers live forever
Escalating on model-reported confidence without calibration: models are often confidently wrong, and the cascade silently ships those answers
Retrying 429s immediately and in lockstep, which turns a rate limit into an outage
Caching responses that contain sampled randomness or tool side effects as if they were pure functions

roles.label: App / gateway
roles.description: Builds the prompt, enforces token budgets and tenant scope, and calls the cache and router.

roles.label: Response cache
roles.description: Exact-match or embedding-similarity store of previous answers, scoped by tenant and prompt version.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: Chooses the model, decides on escalation from a confidence or difficulty signal, and handles fallbacks.

roles.label: Small model
roles.description: Cheap and fast; handles the easy majority of traffic.

roles.label: Large model
roles.description: Expensive and slower; used for hard requests and as the quality backstop.

quiz.question: An internal HR bot sends a 1,500-token system prompt, but each call starts with "Current time: 2026-03-02T14:05:31Z, user: dana" before the instructions. The provider offers prompt-prefix caching and traffic is steady, yet almost no calls get a cached-prefix discount. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the cache time-to-live so prefixes stay stored for hours instead of minutes
Add an exact-match response cache in front of the provider
Move the time and user name to the end, after the stable instructions
Round the timestamp to the nearest minute so more calls share a prefix
quiz.explanation: Traffic is steady, so entries are not expiring; the prefix itself never matches. Prefix caching matches token for token from the start, so any changed token early in the prompt breaks the match for everything after it. Rounding the timestamp still changes the prefix every minute, and a response cache does not help with free-text questions that rarely repeat.

quiz.question: A support bot uses a semantic cache with a cosine similarity threshold of 0.85 and a 60% hit rate. A spot check shows that "Can I cancel within 3 days?" was answered with the cached answer for "Can I cancel within 30 days?". You have no data yet on which threshold is right. What should you do first?
options: Measure wrong hits on labelled near-miss pairs from your traffic, then choose
Raise the threshold to 0.99 and stop, since a near-exact match cannot be wrong
Add a one-hour time-to-live to every entry so wrong answers expire quickly
Scope the cache per user so each person only ever sees their own entries
quiz.explanation: Similarity measures topical closeness, not equivalence, so the threshold has to be chosen from labelled pairs of your own traffic and judged on wrong hits, not only hits. A 0.99 threshold is a guess that also throws away most of the benefit, and a TTL or per-user scope does not stop near-miss questions from matching.

quiz.question: A team routes every question to a small model first and escalates to the large model only when the small model reports confidence below 0.8. The small model costs a twentieth as much and 90% of questions are easy. After launch the bill drops by 85%, but complaints about wrong billing answers rise, and logs show the small model reported 0.95 on many of them. What is the underlying problem?
options: The small model is truncating answers because of the output token cap
Cheap models cannot safely be used in any cascade for billing questions
The cascade retries the small model several times before it escalates
The model's confidence is not calibrated, so wrong answers pass
quiz.explanation: Models are often confidently wrong, so an uncalibrated self-reported score lets bad answers through quietly. Truncation or retries would not explain confidence of 0.95 on wrong answers. The fix is a better signal, such as a verifier, a calibrated score or a classifier checked on labelled data, not abandoning the cascade.
